summary: This memo describes a model for gathering and reporting operational statistics on the Internet, with recommendations for metrics, measurement, polling intervals, storage, and presentation. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 1857.

plainLanguage.summary: To keep a network healthy you need to measure it regularly, like a doctor checking pulse. This paper suggests what to measure, how often, and how to show the results.

questions: what metrics should network operators collect
what is the operational statistics model
which network metrics should be polled
how often should snmp counters be polled
what is data aggregation in network statistics
subtitle: A 1993 proposal for which network metrics to collect, how often, how to store them and how to report them.

tldr.problem: Network operators collected their own metrics in their own ways, so data could not be compared between networks and there was no agreement on what to collect or show.
tldr.mechanism: The memo recommends a minimal set of metrics from the Internet Standard MIB, polling every 60 seconds or a multiple of it, a common text storage format with aggregation, and a few standard report types.
tldr.outcome: The model aims to let network operation centers share statistics easily. The memo is Informational and was replaced by RFC 1857.

today: RFC 1404 is an Informational memo that was obsoleted by RFC 1857, so the newer document is the one to read for this model.

sections.title: The Problem and the Model
sections.content:
Many network administrations collect and archive metrics showing utilization, growth and outages. The goal is near-term problem isolation and longer-term network planning, and also cooperation between networks. Different measurement and presentation techniques make it hard to compare data, and there is no agreement on what to collect or how to display it.

The memo proposes an agreed model with four parts: a minimal set of metrics, tools to collect them, a common storage format, and common presentation formats. Collection tools store data in the common format and presentation tools read it later. Old tools can be retrofitted using conversion filters. The main purpose is to help network operation centers (NOCs) share their statistics with minimal development effort.
sections.plainLanguage: Every school keeps its grades in a different way, so you cannot compare them. This paper suggests everyone measure the same things and write them down the same way.

sections.title: Choosing the Metrics
sections.content:
The memo groups metrics into four measurement areas: utilization, performance, availability and stability. It also groups them by how easily they can be retrieved: variables already in the Internet Standard MIB, variables in private enterprise MIBs, variables needing high resolution polling, and metrics that cannot be retrieved with SNMP at all, such as round-trip delays.

As a minimal set, the memo chooses metrics that are in the Internet Standard MIB. For each interface these are ifInOctets, ifOutOctets, ifInUcastPkts, ifOutUcastPkts, ifInNUcastPkts, ifOutNUcastPkts, ifInDiscards, ifOutDiscards and ifOperStatus. For each node they are ipForwDatagrams, ipInDiscards and sysUpTime. Presence in the Standard MIB is treated as a mandatory requirement.
sections.plainLanguage: Pick a short list of things that every network can already tell you, such as how much came in, how much went out and whether the line is up.

sections.title: Polling and Aggregation
sections.content:
To catch peaks, the traffic counters should be polled at a period of at most 1 minute (60 seconds). If that is not possible, an even multiple of 60 seconds is recommended. The other variables can be polled at a lower rate, again preferably an even multiple of 60 seconds. The memo stresses that all polling and saving values are recommendations and not mandatory.

Polling every minute creates a lot of data, so the memo proposes aggregation: combining entries into longer periods while also storing the peak value of the earlier period so peaks are not lost. Suggested periods are 15 minutes for a 24 hour period, 1 hour for a 1 month period and 1 day for a 1 year period. The memo also advises not storing counters that are not changing, for example on a link that is down, and converting interface data into the resource of interest such as a given link.
sections.plainLanguage: Checking every minute makes a huge pile of numbers. So later you squash old numbers into hourly or daily summaries, but you remember the busiest moment so nothing important is lost.

sections.title: The Storage Format
sections.content:
Statistical data is stored in three kinds of section, each delimited by a BEGIN and END pair: a label section giving start and end times (in UTC) and the data file, a device section describing what is logged, and a data section holding the values. A data section corresponds to exactly one label section and one device section. Sections may appear more than once in a file, and label and device sections can be stored in separate files. How files are physically arranged is outside the scope of the memo.

The device section carries the network name, router name, link name, bandwidth value and unit, protocol type (IP, DECNET, X.25 or CLNS), protocol address, time zone and a tag table that names each polled variable with its initial polling period and aggregation period in seconds. A tag class of total or peak separates totals from aggregated peaks. Each data entry holds a timestamp, a tag, the poll delta in seconds since the previous poll, and the values. Counters are stored as delta values and non-counters such as ifOperStatus as absolute values.

The memo estimates storage at 773 Kbytes for one year with 12 variables, using entry sizes of 131, 242, 353 and 464 bytes for 1 minute, 15 minute, 1 hour and 1 day periods.
sections.plainLanguage: Each file starts with a label that says when and where, then a description of what was measured, then the numbers themselves, so anyone can read it later.

sections.title: Reports and Future Ideas
sections.content:
The memo suggests reports covering offered load (total traffic at external interfaces, segmented by customer, and segmented by protocol or application) and resource utilization for links and routers. Reports can be daily, weekly, monthly or yearly depending on whether the need is operations, engineering or capacity planning. For customers, it recommends sorting offered load in decreasing order and plotting the cumulative percentage carried by the top n customers. What counts as a customer is decided locally.

For utilization it suggests showing average and peak values in the same bar, like a peak meter on audio equipment. Section 8 lists future ideas: a client/server system for exchanging statistics over a TCP based protocol, a subtree in the Internet Standard MIB for operational statistics variables, and detailed per application and per protocol statistics, mentioning the NSF NNStat tool.

On security, section 2.4 notes legal, ethical and political concerns about sharing data, and the need for integrity, conformity and confidentiality of shared data.
sections.plainLanguage: Once the numbers are saved, you draw simple charts: who used the most, and when was it busiest. Showing the average and the peak together helps spot crowded times.

items.title: Utilization
items.text: Total input and output packets and octets, peaks, per protocol and per application.

items.title: Performance
items.text: Delays, collisions, ICMP Source Quench messages and dropped packets.

items.title: Availability
items.text: Line availability as percentage uptime, route and application availability.

items.title: Stability
items.text: Fast line status transitions, route flapping and next hop count stability.
